title: Josiah's Passover and Death
overview: 2 Chronicles 35 details King Josiah's faithful observance of the Passover in Jerusalem, marking a significant religious revival in Judah. Josiah meticulously organizes the priests, Levites, and people to celebrate the Passover according to the Law of Moses, demonstrating his commitment to restoring true worship. The chapter also records Josiah's tragic death in battle against Pharaoh Necho of Egypt, highlighting the consequences of disobedience to God's warning. This chapter serves as a pivotal moment in Judah's history, illustrating the blessings of covenant faithfulness and the judgment that follows rebellion. It emphasizes Josiah's role as a reformer and the solemn reality of divine sovereignty over kings and nations.
structure:
**Verses 1-19: Josiah's Passover Celebration.** This section describes Josiah's detailed preparations and execution of the Passover feast, including the roles of priests, Levites, and singers, as well as the generous offerings made by the king and his officials. It highlights the unprecedented scale and faithfulness of this observance.

**Verses 20-24: Josiah's Battle and Death.** After the Passover, Josiah confronts Pharaoh Necho at Megiddo despite a divine warning delivered through Necho's message. Josiah is mortally wounded, brought back to Jerusalem, and mourned by all.

**Verses 25-27: Josiah's Legacy and Records.** The chapter concludes by noting Jeremiah's lamentations for Josiah and references to written records of Josiah's deeds, emphasizing his lasting impact and the historical documentation of his reign.

keyVerses.text: And there was no passover like to that kept in Israel from the days of Samuel the prophet; neither did all the kings of Israel keep such a passover as Josiah kept, and the priests, and the Levites, and all Judah and Israel that were present, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
keyVerses.significance: This verse underscores the exceptional nature of Josiah's Passover, highlighting his dedication to restoring proper worship and obedience to God's law, setting a high standard for covenant faithfulness.

keyVerses.text: But he sent ambassadors to him, saying, What have I to do with thee, thou king of Judah? I come not against thee this day, but against the house wherewith I have war: for God commanded me to make haste: forbear thee from meddling with God, who is with me, that he destroy thee not.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals God's sovereign control over nations and His direct intervention in political affairs, warning Josiah to avoid conflict that would lead to his downfall.

keyVerses.text: His servants therefore took him out of that chariot, and put him in the second chariot that he had; and they brought him to Jerusalem, and he died, and was buried in one of the sepulchres of his fathers. And all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah.
keyVerses.significance: Josiah's death marks the tragic end of a godly king's reign, emphasizing the cost of disobedience and the deep mourning of the nation for a righteous leader.

keyVerses.text: So kill the passover, and sanctify yourselves, and prepare your brethren, that they may do according to the word of the LORD by the hand of Moses.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the importance of obedience to God's commands as revealed through Moses, underscoring the covenantal faithfulness Josiah sought to restore.

characters.name: Josiah
characters.description: The king of Judah who leads a significant religious reform by organizing a grand Passover celebration according to the Mosaic Law. His dedication to restoring true worship is evident, though his later disobedience leads to his death in battle.

characters.name: Pharaoh Necho
characters.description: The king of Egypt who warns Josiah not to interfere with his military campaign, claiming divine sanction. His encounter with Josiah results in the latter's fatal wounding.

characters.name: Priests and Levites
characters.description: Religious leaders who are assigned specific roles in the Passover celebration, including offering sacrifices, teaching, and leading worship, demonstrating the restoration of proper temple service.

characters.name: Jeremiah
characters.description: The prophet who laments Josiah's death and whose lamentations become an established ordinance in Israel, reflecting the nation's grief and recognition of Josiah's godly leadership.

themes.description: Josiah's Passover represents a renewal of Israel's covenant with God, emphasizing obedience to the Law and wholehearted worship, which is central to the biblical narrative of God's relationship with His people.

The chapter contrasts Josiah's initial obedience in restoring the Passover with his later disobedience in battle, illustrating the blessings of faithfulness and the consequences of ignoring God's warnings.
God's control over nations and history is evident in Necho's warning and Josiah's fate, reinforcing the biblical theme that God directs the rise and fall of kings according to His purposes.

The detailed description of the Passover rituals highlights the importance of proper worship and sacrifice as prescribed in the Law, reflecting God's desire for holiness and reverence among His people.

historicalContext: This chapter is set in the late 7th century BC during the reign of King Josiah of Judah, a time marked by religious reform and political upheaval. Josiah sought to restore the worship of Yahweh in Jerusalem after a period of idolatry and neglect. The Passover celebration described reflects ancient Israelite customs rooted in the Mosaic Law, emphasizing sacrificial rituals and communal participation. Politically, Judah was caught between the rising powers of Egypt and Babylon, with Pharaoh Necho's campaign against Assyria impacting Josiah's reign and ultimately leading to his death at Megiddo. This context highlights the tension between faithfulness to God and the geopolitical realities of the ancient Near East.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes Josiah's Passover as a model of covenant renewal and the necessity of faithfulness to God's law. Josiah's death is seen as a sober reminder of the consequences of disobedience despite initial zeal.

Dispensationalists often view Josiah's reforms as part of Israel's historical cycle of apostasy and revival, with his death marking a transition toward the Babylonian exile and God's unfolding prophetic plan.
Early Church Fathers interpreted Josiah's Passover as a foreshadowing of Christ's ultimate sacrifice and the true Passover Lamb, highlighting the importance of spiritual purification and obedience.

application: Commit to regular renewal of your faith through obedience to God's Word, just as Josiah restored the Passover.
Recognize the importance of corporate worship and the role of church leaders in guiding God's people.
Heed God's warnings and counsel, understanding that disobedience can lead to serious consequences.

Trust in God's sovereign control over all circumstances, including political and personal challenges.
conclusion: 2 Chronicles 35 vividly portrays King Josiah's faithful restoration of the Passover and his tragic death, underscoring the blessings of covenant obedience and the dangers of disregarding God's warnings. Josiah's example challenges believers to pursue wholehearted worship and obedience, while his fate reminds us of God's sovereign authority over history. The chapter encourages the church to uphold faithful teaching, reverent worship, and trust in God's providence, making it a timeless call to covenant faithfulness and reverence for God's commands.
